“Rosalinde”, plate from the Gazette du Bon Ton

George Barbier’s fashion plate of a Worth evening dress, set against a black lacquered commode with gilt mounts, above a centered title in spaced capitals.

Context

The Rijksmuseum lists the plate as Gazette du Bon Ton 1922, No. 10, plate 75: “Rosalinde / Robe du soir, de Worth”, after a design by George Barbier, printmaker anonymous, published by Lucien Vogel with Condé Nast. It describes the technique as photomechanical colour print with letterpress text, sheet 246 × 189 mm. Commons copy of the Rijksmuseum record.

The Rijksmuseum describes the dress as gold lace decorated with pearls. Rijksmuseum.

Observed

  • A slim woman with pale skin and blonde hair in a low knot stands at the center, facing left, her hands on the top of a commode.
  • Her dress is a straight, dropped-waist shift in gold with a diamond pattern, a belt of small geometric blocks in pink and green, and long fringes in blue, green, and gold.
  • The commode behind her is black with gilt rococo mounts and painted pink roses; a blue bowl with a large flower stands at left and a small bronze nude on a marble base at right.
  • The ground is plain cream paper with no setting beyond the furniture.
  • The title “ROSALINDE” is centered below in widely spaced serif capitals, above a smaller line “ROBE DU SOIR, DE WORTH”.
  • Italic lines at the lower corners read “No 10 de la Gazette” and “Année 1922. — Planche 75”. The signature “GEORGE BARBIER 1922” sits at lower left of the image.

Why it belongs

The plate is early, pre-1925 Art Deco: the figure is elongated and simplified, the dress is geometric, and the black lacquer and gold give the luxury palette. The commode itself is an eighteenth-century form, which shows how Deco borrowed historical luxury.

The centered title in spaced capitals on plain ground is the typographic habit later seen in Deco posters and packaging.

Borrow

Center a short title in widely spaced capitals on plain ground, with a smaller second line below it.

Put one glossy black shape behind a light figure to create the lacquer-and-gold contrast.
